strengths: Introduces MeanFlow models as policy representations for online MaxEnt RL, a novel and well-motivated direction for efficient diffusion-style policies.

Proposes an average divergence network to approximate the action likelihood integral, with a principled MeanFlow-style training target and Skilling-Hutchinson trace estimator; empirically validated for accuracy and low overhead.
Develops adaptive instantaneous velocity estimation using two SNIS proposals and ESS-based combination, with bias/variance analysis and ablation support.

Extensive empirical evaluation across MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, HumanoidBench, AntMaze, toy example, and multiple ablations, comparing against numerous diffusion and classical baselines with 5 seeds.
Demonstrates substantial efficiency gains in sampling steps (2 vs 16-20 for many baselines) and training time, while maintaining competitive or better returns.
Reproducibility is generally good: algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware, code link, and implementation details are provided; limitations and impact are discussed.
weaknesses: Theoretical convergence analysis (Props. B.1-B.2) assumes perfect ADN recovery, K→∞, and π*∈Π; it does not address finite-sample bias, approximation error, or the gap between velocity-field matching and KL minimization, which the authors acknowledge but leave as an assumption.

Inconsistent reporting of FlowRL sampling steps (11 in Table 1 vs. 1 in Table 2) and unclear inference latency accounting: MFPO uses 10 action candidates at evaluation (Table 2), but Table 1 reports per-sample latency, so the effective per-action inference cost is likely much higher than 0.46 ms, weakening the inference-efficiency claim.

Notation and presentation issues: r is used for both ODE time interval start and reward; several equations contain typos/duplications (e.g., Eq. 4 denominator, Eq. 5, Eq. 11 t_i=1/T, ∂_u instead of ∂_a), and the reference list has wrong years/citations (e.g., Chen et al. 2025 for Neural ODEs, Li et al. 2022 vs. 2026), harming readability and reproducibility.

The training-time reduction claim (~50%) is not universal: FlowRL appears faster in Fig. 2(f) though with lower return, and the paper's own ablation diffusion-policy baseline (2.45h) is slightly faster than full MFPO (2.81h); the comparison should be clarified.

Some implementation details are missing or underspecified, including the distributional critic architecture, exact auto-tuning temperature implementation, and how action selection interacts with evaluation latency.
The method still requires two sampling steps and the practical deployment cost of action selection is not discussed, limiting the claimed inference efficiency for real-time control.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-motivated problem: diffusion/flow policies for online RL are expensive because of multi-step iterative generation, and reducing this to a few steps is practically valuable. The framing of the efficiency bottleneck (10-20 steps for most diffusion-policy baselines) is accurate and useful.

Two concrete technical components are proposed and integrated into soft policy iteration: (i) an Average Divergence Network (ADN) that learns the time-averaged divergence to approximate the action log-likelihood without explicit Jacobian traces, and (ii) an Adaptive Instantaneous Velocity Estimation (AIVE) that combines two self-normalized importance-sampling (SNIS) estimators (policy proposal and Gaussian proposal) weighted by their Effective Sample Size. Both ideas are reasonable and are supported by derivations (App. B.1-B.4).

The empirical evaluation is broad: MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite (6 hard tasks), and HumanoidBench (3 high-dimensional tasks), plus ablations, a 2-D toy example, and comparisons against GMM and normalizing-flow policies. This gives reasonable coverage of the claim that MFPO matches or beats diffusion baselines at lower cost.

The efficiency gain in sampling steps (T=2 vs 16-20 for baselines) is a meaningful practical result, and the ablation studies (Fig. 3, App. E.7-E.8) attempt to isolate the contribution of the MeanFlow representation, ADN, AIVE, distributional critic, and temperature tuning.
The limitations section is honest about the remaining dependence on two sampling steps and the plan to reduce to one step.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is poor and undermines reliability. There is a duplicated/garbled equation (Eq. 5 appears twice with nonsensical content), the soft policy improvement equation uses 'Q^{\pi_odd}' and '1/\pi Q' instead of 1/\alpha, Sec. 4.3 has an empty heading, the paper repeatedly writes 'velocity filed'/'divergence filed', and the partial-derivative notation is inconsistent (\partial_{\bm{u}}\delta vs \partial_{\bm{a}}\delta). The reference list contains year mismatches (e.g., RFM cited as 'Li et al., 2022' but listed as 2026; SAC-Flow cited as 2022 in text but 2026 in references) and mis-attributions (Neural ODEs attributed to 'Chen et al. 2025'). This makes several claims hard to verify.

The paper's central claim is efficiency, yet the efficiency comparison is not clean. Evaluation uses test-time action selection: M candidate actions are generated and the one with highest estimated Q is chosen (M=10 for MFPO). This is a critic-dependent test-time trick that can inflate returns, and its cost is not reflected in the reported inference latency ('per sample', 0.46 ms), which would effectively become ~10x (~4.6 ms) if the action-selection cost were included—potentially erasing the claimed advantage over baselines.

The timing comparison is potentially unfair: some baselines (DIME, SAC-Flow, MaxEntDP, DACER) use official JAX implementations, while QVPO, SAC, TD3 are reimplemented by the authors in JAX. Mixing official and reimplemented codebases for wall-clock claims is not a controlled comparison.

There is an internal contradiction in the efficiency claim. The main text states MFPO 'reduces training time by approximately 50%', but the ablation Table 3 reports full MFPO at 2.81h versus a 'Diffusion Policy' baseline at 2.45h—i.e., MFPO is slower in that table. The relationship between the 'Diffusion Policy' ablation baseline and the diffusion baselines in Fig. 2 is unclear, so the headline speed claim is not solidly established.

The theoretical support is weak. The convergence statements in App. B.5 (Props. B.1-B.2) essentially assume unbiased likelihood/velocity estimation and that the Boltzmann target lies in the policy class. The paper itself concedes that 'the minimizer of this objective generally does not coincide with that of the KL divergence in Eq. (4)... we assume that the solutions are close in practice.' Thus soft policy iteration convergence is asserted rather than proved for the actual objective used.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines an existing generative model (MeanFlow), an existing framework (MaxEnt/soft actor-critic), and existing tools (SNIS as in MaxEntDP/SDAC, Skilling-Hutchinson trace estimator). The genuinely new pieces (ADN, ESS-weighted two-proposal SNIS) are sensible engineering but not a conceptual leap.

The ADN introduces a coupled moving target: it must track the divergence of a policy that is itself changing during training, and this stability issue (and its interaction with the likelihood used in both the soft Bellman target and the SNIS weights) is not analyzed beyond an empirical loss/variance plot.

Reported results do not uniformly support the 'comparable or superior' claim; several tasks (e.g., Ant-v3, Hopper-v3) show overlapping curves with baselines, and action-selection budgets differ across methods (MFPO 10, MaxEntDP 10, QVPO 32, others none), which complicates the fairness of the return comparison.

strengths: Novel and timely application of MeanFlow models to online RL, directly addressing the efficiency bottleneck of diffusion-based policies while retaining expressive multi-modal action modeling.

Introduces a technically sound average divergence network (ADN) that leverages the MeanFlow identity to approximate action likelihood with a Skilling-Hutchinson trace estimator and one forward pass, adding only ~5% training overhead (Sec. 4.2, App. E.3).

Proposes adaptive instantaneous velocity estimation via self-normalized importance sampling with two complementary proposals (Gaussian and current policy), weighted by effective sample size, with a bias/variance analysis in App. B.4 and ablation evidence in Fig. 3(c).

Provides extensive empirical validation on MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, and HumanoidBench with 5 seeds; MFPO matches or exceeds diffusion baselines while using only 2 sampling steps versus 10-20 and achieving lower inference latency (0.46 ms vs 0.97-1.68 ms, Table 1).

Includes thorough ablations and diagnostics: average vs instantaneous velocity, ADN vs no divergence, proposal ratios, temperature tuning, distributional critic, action selection, sampling steps, and sample numbers (Figs. 3, 11, 12; Apps. E.7-E.8), plus a 2-D toy example showing 2-step likelihood matching a 1000-step Euler solver (Fig. 5).

Reproducibility is well supported: code available, complete algorithms (Algs. 1-3), shared hyperparameters (Table 2), implementation details and compute resources (App. D), and baseline implementations from official repositories.
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges that MFPO still requires 2 sampling steps and outlines future work to reduce to one step (Sec. 6).
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees are only asymptotic and rely on strong assumptions: exact ADN recovery of likelihood, K→∞ for unbiased SNIS, and the Boltzmann policy lying inside the MeanFlow policy class (App. B.5). Finite-sample behavior and approximation errors are not bounded.

The policy improvement step is not exactly the KL projection of soft policy iteration; the paper itself notes that the minimizer generally does not coincide with Eq. (4) when the Boltzmann distribution lies outside the policy class (Sec. 4.4). Thus the claim of 'principled integration' is somewhat overstated.

ADN likelihood estimation is validated only empirically, with relative error against a 1000-step Euler solver on HalfCheetah (Fig. 6c). There is no formal error propagation analysis showing how ADN inaccuracies affect Q-learning or policy improvement.

Presentation contains several equation-level errors and typos: Eq. (4) uses 1/π and π_odd instead of 1/α and π_old; Eq. (5) is duplicated with a nonsensical line; Eq. (11) defines t_i = 1/T without index i; 'velocity filed' is repeatedly misspelled; the reference list has inconsistencies (e.g., SAC-Flow cited as Zhang et al. 2022 in related work but Zhang et al. 2026 in experiments, and Chen et al. 2025 vs 2018 mismatched).

Baseline comparison fairness is imperfect: some baselines were reimplemented in JAX versus their original frameworks, and no statistical significance tests are reported. Although key hyperparameters are unified, baseline-specific tuning may still differ.

The practical advantage over well-tuned one-step Gaussian policies is still limited by the 2-step sampling requirement; inference is ~3× slower than SAC/TD3 (Table 1), and on some tasks (e.g., Hopper-v3 in Fig. 2e) performance overlaps with classical baselines.

The ESS-weighted combination assumes independence of the two SNIS estimators and variance inversely proportional to ESS; finite-sample ESS estimates are noisy and the weighting scheme is heuristic. Only sample-ratio ablation is provided, not comparisons to alternative combination strategies.
